title: Pyridin-3-carbohydrazide strongly impairs Mayaro and Chikungunya virus replication in vitro

analysis.research_question_and_background: Alphaviruses such as Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) are expanding globally and remain without licensed antiviral therapies, creating an urgent need for effective antiviral agents.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study assessed the antiviral activity of pyridine-3-carbohydrazide (P-3-C) against CHIKV (strain La Reunion, LR) using Vero E6 and U-2OS cell lines.
analysis.methods: Vero E6 or U-2OS cells were infected with CHIKV and treated with P-3-C for 24 hours, after which cell viability and viral replication were measured to determine the 50% cytotoxic concentration (CC50), 50% effective concentration (EC50), and selective index (SI).
analysis.main_results: P-3-C reduced intracellular CHIKV RNA levels by 2 log10 compared with controls and decreased viral RNA release; in Vero E6 cells, the SI was greater than 48.8, while in U-2OS cells, the SI was 6.4.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret P-3-C’s antiviral effect as concentration-dependent and multitargeted, involving inhibition of nsP2 protease (IC50 = 12 μM ± 2) and binding to nsP4 polymerase (Kd = 54 μM ± 1), with molecular docking supporting interaction at catalytic pockets.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings suggest P-3-C may be a candidate antiviral for CHIKV, particularly in cell lines where high selectivity is observed, warranting further evaluation in preclinical models.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study’s evidence strength is moderate due to reliance on in vitro models and variability in selectivity across cell lines, which limits generalizability to in vivo contexts.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated pyridine-3-carbohydrazide (P-3-C) as an antiviral against Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) using Vero E6 and U-2OS cell lines. Treatment with P-3-C for 24 hours significantly reduced intracellular CHIKV RNA by 2 log10 and decreased viral RNA release, with a selective index (SI) greater than 48.8 in Vero E6 cells and 6.4 in U-2OS cells. Mechanistic assays indicated P-3-C inhibits CHIKV nsP2 protease (IC50 = 12 μM ± 2) and binds nsP4 polymerase (Kd = 54 μM ± 1), with molecular docking supporting interaction at catalytic sites. The authors propose a multitarget mechanism of action. While promising, the study’s in vitro focus and cell-line-dependent efficacy limit direct clinical translation, warranting further investigation.

title: Chikungunya fever among Japanese travelers: monthly and yearly trends in imported cases, 2011–2023

analysis.research_question_and_background: Chikungunya poses an increasing threat to travelers from non-endemic regions, but the relationship between local transmission intensity in destination countries and infection risk among Japanese travelers remained insufficiently characterized.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study descriptively characterized imported chikungunya cases in Japan from 2011 to 2023 and compared monthly and yearly trends in imported cases by destination with local incidence in the corresponding destination country.
analysis.methods: The study examined descriptive features of imported chikungunya cases, compared incidence trends among Japanese travelers with local incidence in destination countries, and contrasted destination-specific incidence between high- and low-transmission seasons.
analysis.main_results: Of 155 imported chikungunya cases in Japan during 2011–2023, 112 (72.3%) were associated with travel to Myanmar, India, Indonesia, the Philippines, or Thailand, and the yearly importation rate among travelers returning from Indonesia and Thailand correlated with local rates.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The risk of imported chikungunya infection among Japanese travelers reflected the local epidemiology in destination countries, including both seasonal and long-term patterns, indicating traveler risk is closely tied to destination-level transmission dynamics.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Imported-case data can support risk assessment in destination countries and inform traveler-specific prevention, improved diagnosis, and measures to reduce the risk of autochthonous outbreaks.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its descriptive design and reliance on passive surveillance data, which may underestimate true case counts and lack detailed exposure or clinical information, warranting cautious interpretation of the strength of evidence.

analysis.summary_en: This study analyzed 155 imported chikungunya cases in Japan from 2011 to 2023, finding that 72.3% were linked to travel in Myanmar, India, Indonesia, the Philippines, or Thailand. Yearly importation rates among travelers returning from Indonesia and Thailand correlated with local incidence in those countries. Monthly incidence during high-transmission seasons was 12.3, 7.4, 12.0, and 4.0 times higher than in low-transmission seasons for travelers returning from Myanmar, India, Indonesia, and the Philippines, respectively. The authors conclude that the risk of imported chikungunya infection among Japanese travelers mirrors local epidemiology in destination countries, including seasonal and long-term patterns. They suggest that imported-case data can aid risk assessment, guide traveler-specific prevention, improve diagnosis, and help reduce the risk of autochthonous outbreaks.

title: Chikungunya Virus serological cross-reactivity in co-endemic settings: Mechanisms, Diagnostic implications, and epidemiological consequences

analysis.scope_and_question: The review examines Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) serological cross-reactivity in co-endemic settings, focusing on diagnostic challenges and epidemiological consequences. The central question addresses how biological cross-reactivity, assay-associated non-target reactivity, and diagnostic misclassification affect CHIKV serological assays and surveillance accuracy.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: This is a narrative review that distinguishes three phenomena affecting CHIKV serology: biological cross-reactivity, assay-associated non-target reactivity, and diagnostic misclassification. It applies this framework to CHIKV-related alphaviruses (O'nyong-nyong virus, Mayaro virus, Ross River virus) and unrelated flaviviruses (dengue virus, Zika virus). The review emphasizes the need for layered diagnostic strategies and assay validation in co-endemic regions like Nigeria.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: CHIKV shares antigenic overlap with related alphaviruses (ONNV, MAYV, RRV), supported by shared alphavirus architecture and functional cross-neutralisation. By contrast, CHIKV reactivity in DENV- and ZIKV-associated sera lacks a biological basis and is classified as assay-associated non-target reactivity. Unadjusted seropositivity can inflate or obscure CHIKV transmission estimates, and no single diagnostic platform resolves cross-reactivity for all virus pairs.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The mechanism underlying CHIKV reactivity in DENV- and ZIKV-associated sera remains unresolved and is better classified as assay-associated non-target reactivity. The review highlights that unadjusted seropositivity can distort CHIKV transmission estimates, but does not specify the extent of this distortion or provide quantitative evidence for its impact.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: A layered diagnostic strategy is recommended: molecular detection during the acute phase, antigenically informed and multiplex serology thereafter, and neutralisation-based confirmation where attribution is critical. Strengthening assay validation and confirmatory testing, particularly in African co-endemic settings like Nigeria, is essential for improving diagnostic accuracy and epidemiological inference.

analysis.summary_en: This review addresses Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) serological cross-reactivity in co-endemic settings, focusing on diagnostic challenges and epidemiological consequences. It distinguishes biological cross-reactivity (e.g., with ONNV, MAYV, RRV) from assay-associated non-target reactivity (e.g., with DENV, ZIKV) and highlights diagnostic misclassification as a key issue. The review concludes that CHIKV shares antigenic overlap with related alphaviruses, supported by functional cross-neutralisation, while reactivity in flavivirus-associated sera lacks a biological basis. It emphasizes that unadjusted seropositivity can distort transmission estimates and advocates for a layered diagnostic approach—molecular detection, multiplex serology, and neutralisation-based confirmation—combined with improved assay validation in co-endemic regions like Nigeria.

title: Autoantibodies neutralizing type I interferons underlie a third of cases of Chikungunya virus encephalitis or myelitis

analysis.research_question_and_background: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) infection is typically not life threatening but may, in rare cases, affect the central nervous system (CNS). This study aimed to investigate the role of autoantibodies neutralizing type I interferons in CHIKV-related CNS disease.
analysis.study_design_and_population: In three cohorts of confirmed CHIKV cases from Martinique and Brazil, 20 patients had CNS infection. Autoantibodies neutralizing type I interferons were found in 35% of patients with encephalitis, encephalomyelitis, or myelitis, but were absent in 225 patients without CNS infection.
analysis.methods: Autoantibodies neutralizing type I interferons were identified through assays that measured their ability to neutralize high concentrations of IFN-α2, IFN-α8, and IFN-ω, and the antibodies of one patient also neutralized IFN-β.
analysis.main_results: Autoantibodies neutralizing type I interferons were found in 35% of patients with CNS infection, while they were absent in 225 patients without CNS infection. They neutralized high concentrations (10 to 1,000 ng/mL) of IFN-α2, IFN-α8, and IFN-ω, and the antibodies of one patient also neutralized IFN-β.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study found that autoantibodies neutralizing type I interferons are associated with CNS disease in CHIKV infection, suggesting a novel mechanism by which these autoantibodies may contribute to the pathogenesis of the disease.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings may inform the development of targeted diagnostic tests and therapies for CHIKV patients at risk of CNS complications, as well as improve understanding of immune mechanisms in viral infections.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its focus on specific cohorts and the potential for confounding factors, but the evidence is strong as it directly links the presence of autoantibodies to CNS disease in CHIKV patients.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the role of autoantibodies neutralizing type I interferons in Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) infections that lead to central nervous system (CNS) disease. It found that 35% of patients with CNS infection had these autoantibodies, while they were absent in 225 patients without CNS infection. The presence of these autoantibodies before CHIKV infection increased the risk of CNS disease by ~850-fold compared to the general population. The study highlights a novel mechanism involving autoantibodies in CHIKV-related CNS complications, which may have implications for diagnosis and treatment. However, the findings are based on specific cohorts and may have limitations in generalizability. The evidence is strong due to the direct association observed between autoantibodies and CNS disease.

title: Metagenomic sequencing detects viruses and bacteria in a cross-sectional clinical cohort of undifferentiated febrile illness in Nigeria.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the diagnostic gap in low-resource settings where molecular and microscopy-based tools are insufficient to identify causes of febrile illness, particularly in West Africa. The cohort included patients with undiagnosed febrile illness, and the samples were collected from clinics in Jos.
analysis.methods: Unbiased deep sequencing and metagenomic analysis were performed on RNA extracted from patient sera to identify RNA viruses and potentially pathogenic bacteria. The study explicitly aimed to evaluate the utility of metagenomic sequencing for pathogen surveillance in clinical samples.
analysis.main_results: The study detected five human-infecting viruses in 39 (11%) of the 343 specimens, including hepatitis B virus, human pegivirus, and several anelloviruses. While most identified viruses were unlikely to cause clinical symptoms, their presence validated the sequencing approach.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the detection of viral and bacterial genetic material as proof of concept for metagenomic sequencing in identifying pathogens in febrile illness, demonstrating its potential for surveillance in low-resource settings. analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that metagenomic sequencing could improve early detection of disease outbreaks and expand pathogen surveillance in low-resource areas where diagnostic capacity is limited. analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study acknowledges that metagenomic sequencing is susceptible to contamination and false positives, which may limit the reliability of detected pathogens. analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated unbiased metagenomic sequencing (mNGS) as a diagnostic tool for identifying pathogens in 343 febrile patients in Jos, Nigeria, where diagnostic capacity is limited. Using RNA sequencing of sera, the authors detected five human-infecting viruses in 11% of samples, including hepatitis B virus, human pegivirus, and anelloviruses, while also identifying bacterial genetic material. The approach demonstrated proof of concept for pathogen surveillance but did not detect chikungunya virus or other arboviruses targeted in the study. The authors conclude that mNGS can enhance early outbreak detection and surveillance in low-resource settings, though susceptibility to contamination and false positives limits its reliability. The evidence supports moderate confidence in the utility of mNGS for pathogen discovery but not for specific arbovirus surveillance in this cohort.

title: Antibodies elicited by a chimeric peritrophin antigen reduce Aedes aegypti survival after blood feeding.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Vector-borne diseases transmitted by Aedes aegypti, including dengue, Zika, chikungunya, and yellow fever, represent a persistent and expanding global health threat. Limitations of conventional vector control strategies, such as insecticide use and environmental source reduction, particularly in urban settings, underscore the need for novel and complementary tools.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study investigated mosquito peritrophins as potential targets for vector-directed vaccination by designing and recombinantly expressing a chimeric antigen, PT-3, incorporating immunogenic regions from three Aedes aegypti peritrophins/peritrophin-like proteins. The ability of PT-3 to elicit functional antibodies was evaluated in a bovine host model.
analysis.methods: The chimeric antigen PT-3 was recombinantly expressed and used to immunize a bovine host model. Anti-PT-3 immune sera were assessed for recognition of native mosquito midgut components using ELISA and Western blot assays.
analysis.main_results: Immunization induced a robust antigen-specific humoral response, and mosquitoes fed blood supplemented with immune sera from vaccinated animals showed significantly reduced post-feeding survival compared with controls. Anti-PT-3 immune sera recognized native mosquito midgut components in ELISA and Western blot assays.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Results are consistent with antibody-mediated interference with midgut physiological processes during blood digestion, while no significant effects on oviposition or egg viability were observed among surviving females. Findings provide proof-of-concept that mosquito peritrophins can serve as immunological targets for anti-vector vaccination.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings provide a rationale for further developing peritrophin-targeted strategies, including alternative delivery platforms, as complementary tools for arboviral control.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study did not evaluate effects on oviposition or egg viability beyond survival, limiting conclusions about reproductive fitness impacts. Evidence is moderate due to reliance on a bovine model and absence of human or field-relevant data.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated a chimeric peritrophin antigen (PT-3) as a candidate for anti-vector vaccination against Aedes aegypti, the primary vector of chikungunya, dengue, Zika, and yellow fever viruses. The antigen, designed from three Aedes aegypti peritrophins, was recombinantly expressed and used to immunize a bovine host model. Immunization elicited a robust humoral response, and immune sera significantly reduced mosquito survival after blood feeding while recognizing native midgut components in vitro. No effects on oviposition or egg viability were observed. The findings support peritrophins as immunological targets for vector control and justify further development of peritrophin-targeted strategies as complementary tools for arboviral disease prevention.

Significantly higher numbers of Ae. vittatus were found in cattle shelters, particularly during the wet season, while other species showed distinct habitat preferences. The abundance of adult Aedes mosquitoes peaked during the wet season, whereas during the dry season, they were mainly found in moisture-retaining habitats such as deep ground grooves and beneath bridges. The authors highlight the importance of targeted vector control strategies that account for seasonal variation and resting habitat preferences, recommending strengthened entomological surveillance and seasonally adapted interventions to reduce the risk of Aedes-borne viral disease transmission.

title: Limited IgM seroreactivity to arboviruses in free-ranging black-tufted marmosets (Callithrix penicillata)

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to assess the seroreactivity of free-ranging black-tufted marmosets to arboviruses, particularly in an area where these viruses are endemic in humans. Arboviruses are important causes of human disease, and several species also infect wild animals that may serve as amplifying hosts.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was conducted in urban parks where free-ranging black-tufted marmosets (Callithrix penicillata) reside. A total of 68 marmosets were captured and tested for seroreactivity to arboviruses, including chikungunya virus, in an area where these viruses are endemic in the human population.
analysis.methods: Seroreactivity to arboviruses was assessed using antibody detection methods. Arboviruses genomic sequences were not detected in serum samples, but seroreactive animals were not tested by RT-PCR due to sample limitation.
analysis.main_results: The frequency of putative seroreactivity was low, with 2.94% (2/68) of the captured marmosets seroreactive to chikungunya virus (IgM) and 1.47% (1/68) seroreactive to dengue virus. One marmoset was seroreactive to both viruses.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study demonstrated limited evidence of putative seroreactivity of free-ranging black-tufted marmosets to arboviruses, highlighting the need for further investigation into the role of these animals in arbovirus transmission.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that free-ranging black-tufted marmosets may not be significant amplifying hosts for chikungunya virus, which has implications for understanding the ecology and transmission dynamics of arboviruses in urban settings.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study had limited sample size and did not test seroreactive animals by RT-PCR due to sample constraints, which may affect the strength of the evidence. The confidence in the findings is moderate due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the seroreactivity of free-ranging black-tufted marmosets to arboviruses, particularly chikungunya virus, in an urban area where these viruses are endemic in humans. The research aimed to understand the potential role of these primates in arbovirus transmission. Results showed low seroreactivity rates, with 2.94% of marmosets reactive to chikungunya virus (IgM) and 1.47% to dengue virus. One marmoset was found to be seroreactive to both viruses. The study highlights the limited evidence of seroreactivity in these animals, suggesting they may not be significant amplifying hosts for arboviruses. However, the findings are limited by the small sample size and lack of RT-PCR testing for seroreactive individuals, resulting in moderate confidence in the conclusions.

title: Etiological Spectrum of Acute Febrile Illness in a Tertiary Care Hospital in Assam, India: A Cross-Sectional Study

analysis.research_question_and_background: Acute Febrile Illness (AFI) encompasses a spectrum of conditions marked by fever, often caused by various infectious agents. The aetiological diversity poses challenges in diagnosis and treatment, particularly in regions with limited diagnostic resources.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A hospital-based cross-sectional study was conducted from January 2024 to December 2024 on 1,544 patients who had attended Lakhimpur Medical College and Hospital, North Lakhimpur, Assam, India. Patients with fever (≥ 37.5°C) with or without rash were enrolled.
analysis.methods: Serological investigations for Measles, Rubella, Dengue, Varicella-zoster, Chikungunya viruses, Japanese Encephalitis (JE), Orientia tsutsugamushi, Leptospira, and Hepatitis viruses were performed using Enzyme-linked Immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and Rapid Detection Testing (RDT) kits. Data analysis was performed using both descriptive and inferential methods.
analysis.main_results: Fever was prevalent in all 1,544 (100%) cases, followed by 856 (55.44%) cases of headache, 636 (41.19%) with cough, 476 (30.83%) with vomiting, 347 (22.47%) with abdominal pain, 59 (3.82%) cases with dysentery, 52 (3.37%) with diarrhoea, 46 (2.98%) cases with unconsciousness, and 21 (1.36%) cases presented with rash. The study identified seasonal variations in infection rates, with peaks during the monsoon months.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study underscores the importance of integrated clinical and laboratory approaches in diagnosing AFI. Scrub typhus, leptospirosis, and dengue were identified as major causes, emphasising the need for enhanced surveillance and diagnostic capabilities.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the necessity for improved diagnostic tools and surveillance systems to address the diverse aetiology of AFI, particularly in resource-limited settings. The seasonal variations in infection rates can inform public health strategies for prevention and control.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to a single tertiary care hospital in Assam, India, and may not be generalizable to other regions. The evidence is based on serological testing and is of moderate strength due to the observational nature of the study.

analysis.summary_en: This cross-sectional study conducted in a tertiary care hospital in Assam, India, from January to December 2024 aimed to evaluate the spectrum of pathogens causing Acute Febrile Illness (AFI) with or without rash. The study identified fever as the most prevalent symptom, with seasonal variations noted. While the study found that Scrub Typhus, Leptospirosis, and Dengue were major causes, it emphasized the need for integrated clinical and laboratory approaches for accurate diagnosis. The findings suggest the importance of enhanced surveillance and diagnostic capabilities in resource-limited settings. However, the study's limitations include its focus on a single hospital, which may affect generalizability, and its reliance on serological testing, which may not capture all pathogens. The evidence is of moderate strength due to the observational design.

title: OVERVIEW OF THE MOST FREQUENTLY OCCURRING NOTIFIABLE INFECTIOUS DISEASES IN AMAZONAS BETWEEN 2021 AND 2025

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the public-health need to characterize the burden and trends of notifiable infectious diseases in Amazonas, where geographic, environmental, and climatic factors may influence transmission. It asks for an epidemiological profile of major diseases, including arboviruses such as chikungunya, to inform surveillance and control priorities.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective descriptive study with a quantitative approach was conducted using publicly available epidemiological bulletins from the Amazonas Health Surveillance Foundation (FVS-RCP) covering 2021 to 2025. Only data reported in these bulletins were included.
analysis.methods: The study applied a retrospective descriptive design with quantitative analysis of public surveillance data. Descriptive statistics and temporal trends were generated from the bulletins, but no laboratory assays, sequencing, or interventional protocols were described.
analysis.main_results: Between 2021 and 2025, 391,189 cases of the most recurrent notifiable infections were reported in Amazonas, with 332,019 (84.9%) involving major endemic diseases and 31,402 (8.03%) cases of dengue. Chikungunya accounted for 1,336 (0.3%) cases, alongside smaller numbers for Zika, Oropouche, and Mayaro.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the fluctuations and spikes in incidence as driven by Amazonas’s geographic, environmental, and climatic conditions, coupled with urban expansion. The novelty lies in the integrated temporal description of multiple notifiable diseases, highlighting arbovirus co-circulation and burden.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings underscore the need for strengthened surveillance and targeted control measures for arboviruses like chikungunya in Amazonas, particularly given their co-circulation and the state’s ecological vulnerabilities.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited by its reliance on passive surveillance data, which may underestimate true incidence and lacks laboratory confirmation or detailed clinical characterization. The strength of evidence is therefore low to moderate for drawing causal or precise epidemiological inferences.

analysis.summary_en: This retrospective descriptive study analyzed compulsory notification data from Amazonas Health Surveillance Foundation bulletins (2021–2025) to profile major notifiable infectious diseases, including arboviruses. Among 391,189 reported cases, chikungunya accounted for 1,336 (0.3%) cases, with dengue (8.03%) and other arboviruses (Zika, Oropouche, Mayaro) also present. The authors attribute observed fluctuations to environmental, climatic, and urban factors. While the study provides a broad epidemiological overview, its reliance on passive surveillance data and lack of laboratory confirmation limit the precision and strength of conclusions regarding chikungunya specifically.

title: Evidence of co-circulation and co-exposure to arboviruses and malaria in a longitudinal cohort in Kenya from 2019 to 2022

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the growing public-health concern posed by chikungunya virus (CHIKV), dengue virus (DENV), and malaria in sub-Saharan Africa, where similar clinical presentations complicate diagnosis and control. It asks whether these pathogens co-circulate and co-expose individuals, and what risk factors drive their coexistence.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A longitudinal cohort study followed 4,534 participants from December 2019 to February 2022 in two Kenyan sites: Ukunda on the coast and Kisumu in the west. The design aimed to quantify the burden of co-infections and co-exposures to CHIKV, DENV, and malaria.
analysis.methods: The study measured acute infections and lifetime co-exposure to CHIKV, DENV, and malaria using serological and parasitological assays in a defined cohort over a 27-month period.
analysis.main_results: Acute malarial infection was detected in 15.5% of participants, acute DENV in 0.7%, and acute CHIKV in 0.06%. No acute co-infections were detected, while lifetime co-exposure to DENV and malaria was 0.75%, to CHIKV and malaria was 1.8%, and to all three pathogens was estimated at ~0.2%.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the low prevalence of acute CHIKV and the absence of acute co-infections as evidence of limited immediate clinical overlap, while highlighting measurable lifetime co-exposure that may inform future surveillance strategies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that socioeconomic factors, mosquito prevention, and bed-net use may reduce co-exposure risk, whereas crowding and water containers may increase it, guiding targeted interventions in endemic regions.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study’s abstract-only evidence and lack of detailed methods or statistical power assessments limit the strength of conclusions; further data are needed to confirm risk factors and generalisability.

analysis.summary_en: This longitudinal cohort study in Kenya quantified the burden of co-exposure and co-infection to chikungunya virus (CHIKV), dengue virus (DENV), and malaria among 4,534 participants from December 2019 to February 2022. Acute infections were detected in 15.5% for malaria, 0.7% for DENV, and 0.06% for CHIKV, with no acute co-infections observed. Lifetime co-exposure was 0.75% for DENV and malaria, 1.8% for CHIKV and malaria, and ~0.2% for all three pathogens. The authors link higher socioeconomic status, mosquito prevention, and bed-net use to reduced co-exposure risk, while crowding and water containers may increase it. However, the abstract-only evidence and absence of detailed methods limit the strength of these conclusions.

title: RNA Cis-Elements Involved in Animal Virus Stop Codon Readthrough: Stop Codon Context and Downstream RNA Structures

analysis.scope_and_question: This review focuses on two viral cis-elements that modulate readthrough across four viral genera in which this decoding event has been experimentally validated: (i) primary sequences surrounding the stop codon (stop codon context), and (ii) downstream RNA structures.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review discusses the mechanisms of stop codon readthrough in viruses, including interactions between viral RNA elements and host translational machinery, and the role of ribosomal A-site competition between near-cognate tRNAs and eRF in promoting non-canonical decoding events.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: In eukaryotic systems, interactions with the ribosomal mRNA entry channel have been suggested. These findings may have implications for antiviral strategies targeting these RNA elements.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Effects of stop codon context have been observed more broadly in cellular genes, including nonsense suppression in bacteria, with mechanisms including inefficient RF association or tRNA interactions at adjacent sense codons. This effect has not been consistently observed in chikungunya and triatoviral structures, suggesting a strong dependence on local sequence and structural context.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Understanding the interplay between viral RNA elements and host translational machinery, including potential kinetic trapping at the termination codon, provides insights into this unusual elongation mechanism.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the mechanisms of stop codon readthrough in Chikungunya virus, focusing on cis-elements that modulate this process. It highlights the role of stop codon context and downstream RNA structures in promoting readthrough, which is a noncanonical translation strategy. The review notes that while stop codon readthrough is common in cellular genes, its occurrence in viral systems, particularly in Chikungunya virus, is more consistent and significant. It also discusses the potential implications of these findings for antiviral strategies. However, the effect of stop codon context on readthrough is not consistently observed in all viral genera, indicating a strong dependence on local sequence and structural context. The review emphasizes the importance of understanding the interaction between viral RNA elements and host translational machinery to develop targeted interventions.

title: Estimación del riesgo a la salud por exposición laboral a pesticidas utilizados en el control de vectores en México

analysis.research_question_and_background: El estudio aborda el problema de la exposición laboral a pesticidas utilizados en el control de vectores de enfermedades víricas, como el chikungunya, en México, donde estos agentes constituyen un desafío de salud pública. El objetivo es evaluar el riesgo sanitario asociado con el uso de estos pesticidas en el ámbito laboral.
analysis.study_design_and_population: El estudio se enfoca en la evaluación del riesgo de salud por exposición ocupacional a pesticidas utilizados para el control de vectores de enfermedades víricas en México. Se consideraron los principales pesticidas recomendados por el CENAPRECE, incluyendo bendiocarb, bifentrina y pirimifos-metil, que son potencialmente tóxicos para los seres humanos.
analysis.methods: Se identificaron los efectos sobre la salud de los pesticidas considerando su potencial tóxico (pT) y neurotóxico (pNe), así como la dosis de exposición estimada (DEE) en el ámbito laboral, de acuerdo con los años de exposición. Se calculó el riesgo no cancerígeno individual (HQi) y el índice de riesgo (HI) para cada pesticida.
analysis.main_results: El bendiocarb mostró los valores más altos de riesgo de efectos no cancerígenos sobre la salud, con HQ > 1 (riesgo alto) y incrementos significativos de 1.35, 2.7 y 4.1 conforme aumentaron los años de exposición laboral (5, 10 y 15 años, respectivamente). La bifentrina y el pirimifos metil presentaron incrementos proporcionales al tiempo de exposición laboral, pero con valores de HQ < 1 (riesgo bajo).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Los resultados indican que el bendiocarb representa el mayor riesgo para la salud en comparación con los otros dos pesticidas, lo cual es una observación directa basada en los cálculos de riesgo no cancerígeno individual (HQi) y el índice de riesgo (HI).
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Estos hallazgos pueden informar la necesidad de implementar medidas de protección más estrictas para los trabajadores expuestos al bendiocarb, así como guiar la selección de pesticidas en programas de control de vectores de enfermedades víricas en México.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: El estudio se basa en datos abstractos y no proporciona información detallada sobre la metodología o controles utilizados, lo que limita la confianza en los resultados. Sin embargo, los hallazgos son directos y se basan en cálculos de riesgo no cancerígeno individual (HQi) y el índice de riesgo (HI), lo que justifica una evaluación de confianza moderada.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluates the health risk associated with occupational exposure to pesticides used for vector control in Mexico, focusing on those relevant to chikungunya virus transmission. The research identifies bendiocarb as the pesticide with the highest non-cancerous health risk, based on calculated hazard quotients (HQi) and risk indices (HI), which increase significantly with years of exposure. Bifenthrin and pirimiphos-methyl show proportional increases in risk but remain at lower levels. The findings highlight the need for stricter protective measures for workers exposed to bendiocarb and inform the selection of pesticides in vector control programs. However, the study is limited to abstract-level data, and the evidence is considered moderate in strength due to the lack of detailed methodology and controls.
